analysis.one_liner: Requires banks and other financial firms trading derivatives to meet regulator-set capital, disclosure, and risk-management standards.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on January 4, 1995, referred to the House Banking Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed federal regulators to write common capital, accounting, disclosure, and suitability rules for financial institutions that deal in or heavily use derivatives — the complex contracts whose misuse contributed to bank failures and, years later, the 2008 crisis. It would have required detailed reporting of derivatives holdings in regulatory call reports, barred institutions from trading derivatives without a board-approved risk plan, tightened FDIC handling of swap contracts at failed banks, and ordered a government study of whether speculative derivatives trades should face margin requirements. It never moved past the referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank depositors, bank customers, and taxpayers who stand behind federal deposit insurance. Better capital, disclosure, and internal-control standards for derivatives are meant to reduce the chance of a bank failure that the FDIC — and ultimately taxpayers — must cover, and to give regulators early warning of dangerous positions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs federal regulators to establish substantially similar capital, accounting, disclosure, risk-management, and suitability standards for financial institutions engaged in derivatives activities, considering factors like capital requirements, stress testing, credit risk reserves, and board oversight.

It requires insured banks and credit unions to disclose the size, terms, and trading gains and losses of their derivative instruments in regulatory call reports, and authorizes comparable quarterly reporting by other financial institutions, so regulators can see exposures that are otherwise hard to track.
It bars any financial institution from engaging in derivatives without a board-approved written management plan, and lets regulators treat noncompliance as an unsafe or unsound practice.

It expands the FDIC's authority over swap and related contracts when a bank fails and orders a GAO study of speculative derivatives use and whether margin and collateral requirements should be imposed on such trades.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, securities firms, insurance companies, and other institutions that deal in or actively use derivatives would bear compliance costs: new capital charges, detailed reporting, board oversight requirements, and recordkeeping for troubled institutions. Some of those costs could be passed to customers through pricing.

drawbacks.text: Much of the bill directs agencies only to 'consider' and 'may require' standards rather than writing hard rules into law, so its force would depend heavily on how regulators implemented it.

New capital, margin, and reporting requirements raise compliance costs for financial institutions, which can be passed on to customers and could, in the view of opponents, push some derivatives activity to less-regulated foreign institutions.
The disclosure and internal-control mandates apply broadly — including to credit unions and a wide range of securities and insurance firms — even where derivatives activity is small.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — reducing the risk of hidden derivatives losses toppling insured banks — is real and large, and the direct costs fall mainly on large trading institutions rather than ordinary households. The bill's weakness is design: it delegates most of the hard choices to regulators instead of setting firm rules itself, and its reporting burdens are broad. On balance it is a modest, supervisory approach to a problem that later proved much larger.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Henry Gonzalez, the former chairman of the House Banking Committee, introduced the Derivatives Safety and Soundness Supervision Act of 1995 on January 4, 1995, with two Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services on January 4, 1995; the only other recorded action was the sponsor's introductory remarks the next day.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded for the bill in the 104th Congress, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and derivatives dealers came out ahead: no new capital, disclosure, internal-control, or potential margin requirements were imposed on their derivatives business during this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Henry B. Gonzalez
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-TX); former chair, House Banking Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Reps. Paul Kanjorski and Kweisi Mfume

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services (Chair Jim Leach)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction; new Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — after it was referred on January 4, 1995.

against.name: Large banks and derivatives dealers
against.what_they_did: Opposed new capital, disclosure, and margin requirements for over-the-counter derivatives during this period, and Congress enacted no such rules in the 104th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee that held the bill was controlled by the Republicans who won the majority in 1995.

industries.note: The bill would impose capital, disclosure, internal-control, and emergency-reporting requirements on institutions dealing in or actively using derivatives, and would open the door to margin requirements on speculative trades through the GAO study. Safer balance sheets protect depositors and the deposit insurance fund, but the industry's own interest in this bill ran toward avoiding those costs.

The bill's broad definition of 'financial institution' pulls broker-dealers, investment advisers, and insurers under comparable quarterly derivatives reporting through the SEC, CFTC, and Treasury. The added reporting burden is real but modest relative to what banks face.

Insured credit unions would face the same derivatives disclosure requirements in their call reports as banks. Few credit unions use derivatives significantly, so the burden is small but the requirement is universal.
